item.title: C++ Containers and Iterators
item.description:
Choose a container from the required lookup, traversal, insertion, erasure, memory locality, and reference-stability properties. Complexity describes an operation under its preconditions; invalidation and ownership determine whether a design remains correct after mutation.

Selecting a Container #

  • std::vector is the default sequence for contiguous storage, random access, cache locality, and C interoperation through data(). Appending is amortized constant time. Any capacity growth invalidates every iterator, pointer, and reference; without growth, insertion invalidates iterators and references at or after the insertion point.
  • std::deque supports indexed access. End insertion invalidates iterators but not references; its storage is non-contiguous, and middle insertion invalidates iterators and references.
  • std::list and std::forward_list retain iterators and references to unaffected nodes across insertion and erasure. Their node allocation and pointer chasing make them a measured choice, not a default.
  • std::map and std::set provide ordered traversal and logarithmic lookup. Insertion does not invalidate iterators or references, except erased elements.
  • std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set provide average constant-time lookup. Rehash invalidates iterators, although references and pointers to elements remain valid; erasing invalidates only the erased element.

reserve() avoids predicted vector reallocations and can also reduce unordered_* rehashing. It does not make an iterator valid after an operation whose documented rules invalidate it.

item.title: C++ Random Number Facilities
item.description:
The C++ random library separates a deterministic engine from a distribution. An engine produces a sequence of uniformly distributed values over its specified output range. A distribution consumes engine output and maps it to a requested statistical distribution. Keep both objects alive when their state must continue.

cpp 
#include <random>

std::mt19937_64 engine{std::random_device{}()};
std::uniform_int_distribution<int> die{1, 6};

int roll = die(engine); // Both engine and distribution may advance state.

std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 are pseudo-random engines: a fixed initial state produces a reproducible sequence. std::default_random_engine is implementation-defined, so it is unsuitable when tests, files, or protocols require the same sequence across implementations.

item.title: C++ Ranges and Views
item.description:
The ranges library separates the ability to iterate from ownership, traversal strength, and lazy transformation. A range supplies iteration boundaries; a view is a range suited to adaptor pipelines; an adaptor builds a new view whose elements are evaluated when iteration requests them.

cpp 
#include <ranges>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> source{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
auto even_squares = source
 | std::views::filter([](int value) { return value % 2 == 0; })
 | std::views::transform([](int value) { return value * value; });

Constructing even_squares does not transform every element. Iteration invokes the predicate and transformation, so changes to source before iteration can be observed subject to the source container’s invalidation rules.

item.title: Java Standard Library
item.description:
Small library contracts frequently determine correctness more than API surface area. The following rules prevent common Java integration failures.

Object Contracts #

equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. If two objects are equal, they must have the same hashCode; therefore override both before using a value as a hash key. Do not mutate equality fields while an object is a map key. Prefer composition over inheritance when equality would otherwise break symmetry.
